title: Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka have no respect for law, can breach peace and tranquility: Delhi SEM court
summary: A Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) court on Monday said that Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) activists Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka's conduct shows that they have no respect for the law and that there are serious concerns about them breaching peace and tranquillity. SEM Ritu Raj said that their assurance that they would not repeat the alleged conduct did not inspire confidence in light of their previous actions.The Court said that they showed "habitualness" by calling for protest at de-notified areas.Therefore, the Court extended their judicial custody by two days. "The application filed by IO [Investigating Officer] is supported by substantial material on record, raising serious concerns regarding the likelihood of breach of peace and disturbance of public tranquillity, which cannot be brushed aside without proper consideration," the Court said. Further, the SEM also rejected the sureties produced for Ranka and Das after finding them unfit.It noted a mismatch between the photograph on one of the sureties' bond and his Aadhaar card. The Court said that he [the surety] failed to produce another valid identity document and gave unsatisfactory answers. Meanwhile, according to the Court, the other surety could not provide basic details of Saurav Das. The court also found that neither surety could ensure the respondents’ presence before it. "The inquiry conducted revealed that both the Sureties has no control over the Respondents to produce them before the Court, which is primary essence of keeping Surety. No other Surety present at present. In such a situation, respondents are directed to furnish fresh Sureties," the Court recorded in its order. It has now listed the case for further consideration on October 21.Das and Ranka were detained by the Delhi Police on October 13 after they allegedly entered the barricaded Jantar Mantar site by climbing its gates. On October 14, they were sent to judicial custody for five days. As the custody ended today, they were produced before the SEM. The Delhi Police sought an extension of the custody. The same was allowed and the custody was extended by two more days.The CJP has been protesting alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.When Das and Ranka were produced before SEM today, the police told the court that they had breached an undertaking given before the SEM on October 11. It was stated that they called upon the public to assemble at Jantar Mantar, which has been de-notified as a protest site. The police further alleged that Das and Ranka repeatedly used social media to mobilise people for protests at non-designated locations, including Jantar Mantar and Connaught Place. The police officials also referred to an anonymous allegedly threatening WhatsApp communication received by the predecessor court, stating that a separate daily diary entry had been registered in connection with it. Opposing further detention, counsel for the respondents argued that they should be released immediately and assured the court that they would not repeat the alleged conduct. They also disputed the allegation that they had issued calls for protests after October 10.

title: YSR Congress moves Supreme Court alleging candidates blocked from filing nominations for municipal polls
summary: The YSR Congress Party (YSRCP) has moved the Supreme Court alleging that poll violence blocked its candidates from filing nominations for the upcoming Andhra Pradesh's urban local body elections.The plea challenges an order passed by the Andhra Pradesh High Court refusing to extend the deadline for filing nominations.A vacation Bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana of the apex court will hear the plea on October 21. That is also the last date for withdrawal of candidature. Polling is scheduled for October 28.The party first moved the High Court on October 10, before the polls were notified, seeking secure additional nomination centres. A single-judge dismissed that plea on October 15.Subsequently, it moved the High Court flagging violence at nomination centres and seeking extension of deadline to file nominations.On October 18, a division bench of the High Court comprising Justices Ninala Jayasurya and Purushottam Kumar Chintalapudi rejected the party's plea for a one-day extension to file nominations. The High Court said that the time for filing nominations had expired and any direction to extend the same would amount to interference with the election process.This prompted the plea before the Supreme Court.As per the petition, there was violence at Punganur and Rayachoti on October 16, the first day of nominations. A candidate's papers were snatched and torn at Kadapa, and candidates in Tirupati were assaulted and prevented from reaching nomination centres. Nine Tirupati candidates have filed affidavits saying they were obstructed while trying to file their nominations.The petition argues that the principle of non-interference with elections is only a rule of judicial restraint and not an absolute bar on court's intervention.According to the plea,"In a situation where the democratic process is being thwarted, it is the bounden duty of the Constitutional Courts to step in and ensure that elections take place transparently and that no candidate is forced out of the race."Further, the expiry of time was itself the consequence of the obstruction complained of, and could not be a ground to deny relief, it has been contended.The plea has sought the following reliefs:- extension of the nomination period;- additional nomination centres with videography;- police protection for candidates; and- a stay on unopposed declarations.The petition was filed through advocate Mahfooz A Nazki.

title: Remembering the forgotten ones: Veteran Supreme Court lawyers recall AoRs, lawyers of yesteryear
summary: Doyens of the Supreme Court Bar recently reminisced the past, recalling lesser-known lawyers and Advocates-on-Record (AoRs) forgotten in days gone past.Moderated by Senior Advocate K Parameshwar, the discussion featured veteran Senior Advocates KK Venugopal, Raju Ramachandran and CS Vaidyanathan, as well as former Supreme Court Justice BP Singh.The panel also spoke about the agent system that was a precursor to the AoR mechanism, lawyers-turned-politicians and more.[Watch Video]Venugopal recalled the late R Gopalakrishnan, father of Senior Advocate Gopal Subramanium, who was his AoR right through from the 1960s until he passed away. The former Attorney General recounted an instance when Gopalakrishnan appeared in court despite suffering from internal bleeding.“He went about asking for adjournment on the last day, saying I have to have an operation. He told the Chief Justice that he was bleeding internally. And the Chief Justice was horrified. And nevertheless, he was trying to handle cases from court to court. Chief Justice said, Gopal, listen, do you know what you are doing with your life? You better go straight away. I won't listen to you for a moment.”The other names recalled by the panel included JB Dadachandji, Naunit Lal, Nuruddin Ahmed, AG Ratnaparkhi, Ganpat Rai, Arun Bahadur Saharya, RB Datar and BR Agarwala. Recalling Agarwala, Ramachandran said,“He was an avid book collector and he had a great work-life balance and he was a very efficient work manager…He would finish his work every day by around 6 o'clock, spend half an hour wandering around the second-hand bookshops of Connaught Place looking for a rare book to add to his collection. And he had an amazing private library...So among the books in his library was a fabulous collection of Kama Sutras in different languages published across the world. I didn't attempt to look, but I saw the shelf, which he proudly showed me!”Justice Singh spoke of a time when “agents” would manage cases in the Supreme Court before the formalised AoR system. The agents, who were not necessarily law graduates, would manage the cases. They corresponded with the lawyers, but they were not allowed to address the court, he said.“Then the judges decided that we should discontinue this agency and have AoRs When they said on record, they wanted to have a separate record of the advocates in the Supreme Court for the reason that we have cases from all over the country. So, they insisted that you have an office within the 10 kilometres of the Supreme Court. That was one. And two, that there should be law graduates. So, all those agents who were law graduates became advocates on record.”The panelists also discussed the relationship between senior advocates and AoRs back in the day, with Vaidyanathan recounting,“When there was criticism, something is missing, etc, they (senior advocates) would take it upon themselves. Unlike some of the seniors today, they were so generous and protective of the advocates on record. They would never expose the faults of the advocates on record.”The discussion moved on to lawyers-turned-politicians and the panelists listed Bengali lawyers who went to serve in positions with the government. They spoke of Somnath Chatterjee, Ashoke Sen, Siddhartha Shankar Ray, Sachindra Chaudhuri, Debi Prasad Pal and Sankar Ghose.Parameshwar then pointed out that Venugopal had two Cabinet Ministers – P Chidambaram and Rangarajan Kumaramangalam - working with him in chambers. Responding to a question on whether they indulged in politics during their time in chambers, Venugopal said,“No. See, when the emergency was declared, I was appearing for Karunanidhi challenging the dismissal of the government, alleging malafides against Indira Gandhi. They straight away had to leave my chambers…And at one time, when I was appearing in other emergency cases, when they were detained in Bangalore. When I went to Delhi, I was told that some IB man was inquiring as to which was my home and so on.Therefore, I was under the impression that it could be possible that along with all the other lawyers who had been detained, I could be with them. But I believe that these two former juniors of mine were responsible for telling the government that look, this will be a very wrong thing because so far as the Madras Bar is concerned, it has not been raising its voice against the Emergency. But if you do something, arrest him or raid him, then there may be a reaction.And I said, I don't mind the raid because all that they will find is an extra bottle of whisky, more than my permit permitted!”

title: Forgery by police in forgery case: Allahabad High Court orders perjury probe
summary: The Allahabad High Court has directed its Registrar General to probe the fabrication of an arrest memo submitted by the police in response to a habeas corpus petition alleging irregularities in the arrest of a man accused of forgery [Junaid and another v. State of UP and 4 Others]A Bench of Justices Atul Sreedharan and Achal Sachdev found that the arrest memo submitted before the trial court at the time of remand was different from the one submitted by the police before the High Court.The Court found that the police added grounds of arrest to the arrest memo after the remand proceedings and "perhaps" after the filing of the habeas corpus petition."It is necessary to mention here that in the original arrest memo, this was never entered into by the I.O. and in order to perfect the arrest memo, perhaps after the habeas corpus petition was filed before this Court, by fabricating entries in Item Nos.12 and 13 of the second page of the arrest memo, which clearly reflect that fabricated document was placed before this Court along with the counter affidavit," the Court said.Justice Atul Sreedharan and Justice Achal SachdevThe Court was dealing with the habeas corpus plea moved by one Junaid, who was arrested by the Aligarh police on August 6. He alleged that the arrest memo provided to him did not have the grounds of arrest and thus his custody was in violation of the guidelines laid down by the Supreme Court.During the hearing, Junaid's counsel produced a certified copy of the arrest memo placed before the remand magistrate. He also pointed to the additions made to the arrest memo filed by the police in its response to the habeas corpus plea.On comparing the two documents, the High Court observed that the grounds of arrest mentioned in the original arrest memo were "perfunctory". It added the document filed before the High Court was fabricated."The certified copy reflects that the unfabricated original document that was placed before the Magistrate at the time of the remand. Thus, it is clear that the fabrication in the said document has been done by the police on a date after the remand proceedings and perhaps after the habeas corpus petition was filed," the Court said.The Court noted that the documents may have been fabricated by the investigating officer. Taking a serious note of the offence committed by the police, the Court passed the following direction:"This Court considers it necessary to direct the Registrar General of this Court to proceed under Section 379 of BNSS for cases mentioned in Section 215 of BNSS, as the offence has been committed in a judicial proceeding. After the inquiry, if the Registrar General is satisfied that prima facie, an offence relating to fabrication of documents and perjury has been committed before this Court, on the basis of perusal of the documents/records of this case, in such an eventuality, he shall do the needful and file a case before the Court of competent jurisdiction against those found prima facie involved in the offence." Concluding that the grounds of arrest given to the accused were inadequate, the Court ordered his release. Senior Advocate Mohit Singh and advocate Subir Lal represented the petitioner.[Read Order]

title: PIL in Calcutta High Court alleges State fraudulently issuing stamp papers to garner numbers for TMC rebel faction
summary: The Calcutta High Court on Tuesday sought a response from the West Bengal government to a public interest litigation (PIL) petition alleging that the State in cahoots with police and other authorities is fraudulently distributing stamp papers and forcefully obtaining signatures of Trinamool congress (TMC) members and others to support rebel members and leader of opposition Ritabrata Banerjee's faction [Surajit Mondal v. State of West Bengal and Ors.].A division bench of Chief Justice Ravindra Vithalrao Ghuge and Justice Shabbar Rashidi said that stamp papers can be sold only by licensed vendors and such sale must be properly recorded."Stamp papers can only be sold by licensed stamp vendors. The sale of stamp papers must be there in the register. Show us whether you are doing this," the Court said.The State said it will file a detailed response and sought time for the same.The court agreed and posted the case for further consideration on December 11. The petition before the Court was filed by one Surajit Mondal, an elected member of the Zilla Parishad in Hooghly.The dispute arose from opposition leader Ritabrata Banerjee's claim that his rebel faction is the original TMC party which entitles him to the "Flower and Grass" symbol used by Mamata Bnerjee's faction. Ritabrata Banerjee had broken away from Mamata Banerjee's TMC and earlier this year and has been claiming that he represents the real TMC since he has the support of more MLAs. He was later recognised as the leader of opposition by the speak of West Bengal assembly.The dispute over which faction is the real TMC is pending before the Election Commission of India (ECI) and signatures on stamp papers is crucial to proving which faction has greater numbers.This would thus affect the outcome of the dispute before ECI.According to the petition, the upper echelons of the State government have instructed local authorities across West Bengal to unlawfully order the distribution of stamp papers, and existing TMC members and others have been coerced to give their signatures for the cause of the rebel faction.Senior Advocate Kalyan Bandopadhyay, appearing for the petitioner, said that lakhs of stamp papers have been issued without making serialized entries of the issuance of the papers in the appropriate registers.He said that the Court should call for a report from the State detailing the entries of stamp papers in the requisite sub-registries.The State, on the other hand, challenged the maintainability of the PIL but sought time to seek instructions from the concerned departments. The Court then asked State to file its response.The issue pertaining to the maintainability of the petition remains to be argued at length. "Since the issue of maintainability has been raised, the Respondents are at liberty to file their specific objection with regard to the maintainability of the PIL, along with their reply, with proper pagination in continuation with the petition," the Court said in its order.Senior Advocate Kalyan Bandopadhyay and advocates Suman Sengupta, Anit Kumar Das, Ashish Dutta and Rahul Kumar Singh appeared for the petitionerGovernment Pleader DN Ray with advocates Anindya Basu, Pradip Mukherjee, Indradeep Pal and Bikash Kumar Sriwastav represented the State.[Read Order]

title: Allahabad High Court asks Centre, RBI to frame guidelines to deal with bank accounts of persons in coma
summary: The Allahabad High Court has asked the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to consider framing guidelines to deal with bank accounts held by persons in a coma [Parveen Jahan v State of UP and Another]A bench of Justice Ajit Kumar and Justice Garima Prasad expressed concern that the dependents of such patients are left without any legal remedy, as they cannot access the funds held in their bank accounts,The Court directed the Central government and the RBI to disclose what they propose to do in this regard or place on record any existing guidelines to attend to such cases of special nature. “Some sort of legislation from the competent legislature or even the guidelines necessary from the Reserve Bank of India regulating the nationalised bank and subsidiary banks to the nationalised banks for providing necessary mechanism as to how the money lying in the savings bank account of such patients can be released in favour of the dependents. The Central Government, therefore, has to come up with its stand on the issue in black and white. We also need Reserve Bank of India to give its response on the above issue,” the Court said.Justice Ajit Kumar and Justice Garima PrashadThe Court was dealing with a petition filed by a woman seeking to withdraw money lying in the bank account of her husband, who was in a coma. The man died during the pendency of the plea.Considering the larger question raised in the case, the Court asked the Central government and RBI to address the issue at the earliest.“The Reserve Bank of India and the Central Government will have to file their respective affidavits, failing which the Court will be compelled to summon the responsible officers of both the Central Government as well as Reserve Bank of India,” the Court said on October 8.The matter will be heard next on November 6. In the meantime, the Court said that the State can consider enforcement of the guidelines framed by the Kerala High Court in Shobha Gopalakrishnan v. State of Kerala. It said the Chief Secretary must come up with something concrete and substantial at his level. “We make it clear that if the Chief Secretary does not come up with such solution in black and white, he will have to appear in person before this Court on the next date fixed,” the Court said.Advocate Raj Kumar Dhama represented the petitioner.[Read Order]

title: Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka move Delhi High Court against judicial custody
summary: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) activists Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka have approached the Delhi High Court against a special executive magistrate (SEM) court order sending them to judicial custody till October 21. They have alleged that their continued detention violates their fundamental right to liberty.The CJP's legal head, Ratna Singh, said they would be seeking an urgent hearing and would request the Court to get the matter listed today.Notably, the Delhi Police detained Das and Ranka on October 13 after they allegedly entered the barricaded Jantar Mantar site by climbing its gates. On October 14, they were sent to judicial custody for five days. On October 19, the custody was extended for two more days. In its October 19 order, the SEM court said that Das and Ranka's conduct showed that they have no respect for the law and that there are serious concerns about them breaching peace and tranquillity. It held that their assurance that they would not repeat the alleged conduct did not inspire confidence in light of their previous actions.The Court said that they showed "habitualness" by calling for protest at de-notified areas.Further, the SEM also rejected the sureties produced for Ranka and Das after finding them unfit. It noted a mismatch between the photograph on one of the sureties' bond and his Aadhaar card. The Court said that he [the surety] failed to produce another valid identity document and gave unsatisfactory answers. The other surety could not provide basic details of Saurav Das. The Court also found that neither surety could ensure the respondents’ presence before it. Das and Ranka have now approached the High Court against their custody.In this petition, Das and Ranka have contended that they have remained in custody for six days despite repeatedly furnishing sureties.They have argued that the magistrate wrongly extended their judicial custody under Section 135(3) BNSS on the ground that they had defaulted in executing the required bond, despite their sureties having been produced in accordance with law.The plea states that the SEM order mechanically relies on the police's application without recording an independent assessment of the circumstances warranting continued custody. Further, they argue that a protest at a denotified site is, at its highest, a question of regulation, not a threat to public order. "That a restraint on the liberty of the Petitioners founded on an apprehension of breach of tranquillity or public order and attributed to them, must satisfy the test of Article 19(3) of the Constitution," the plea states.On the issue of surety, they rely on a 2018 Delhi High Court judgment in Aldanish Rein v State of NCT of Delhi to argue that a person should be released on a personal bond while verification of the sureties is pending.The plea further alleges that the magistrate rejected their sureties on grounds that they could not guarantee the petitioners’ appearance before the court and could not recall their parentage. The CJP activists contend that Section 140 BNSS permits rejection of a surety only if the person is found unfit for the bond. They have also argued that the magistrate failed to specify the number of sureties, the bond amount and the duration of the bond, as required under Section 130 BNSS.

title: Calcutta High Court dismisses CPI(M)'s plea to halt removal of temporary book stall
summary: The Calcutta High Court on Tuesday dismissed the Communist Party of India (Marxist)'s [CPI(M)] plea to halt the removal and dismantling of a temporary book stall near the Jadavpur coffee house during Durga Puja despite making the requisite application and paying a fee to the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) [Communist Party of India (Marxist) v. State of West Bengal & Ors.]. Justice Partha Pratim Roy observed that making the requisite application and paying the fee to the local authorities for operating a temporary book stall is not enough without explicit permission for operating such a stall."In view of the law laid down by the Hon’ble Division Bench in MAT 1881 of 2026, a person who approaches the Court will have to be first established whether the said party has a permission for erecting a stall or not. Therefore, the protection as sought for by the petitioner requires establishing, that they had a valid permission to run the bookstall. In the present case, such permission is absent. In view of the law declared by the Hon’ble Division Bench, the writ petitioner is not entitled to any relief as prayed for," the Court said.CPI(M) moved the Court after some people, allegedly belonging to the KMC and accompanied by a large police contingent and a bulldozer, attempted to remove the stall on October 17.CPI(M) had been operating the temporary book stall in front of the Jadavpur coffee house during Durga Puja for the last 49 years.Keeping up with the same practice, they applied for permission to set up the book stall to the office of Assistant Director SWM-I, Borough – X, Kolkata Municipal Corporation. A fee amounting to ₹3,208 was also paid to the concerned KMC department in this regard. A letter to that effect was also sent to the concerned officer-in-charge of the nearby police station . After examining the facts of the case, the Court observed, "Running of the aforesaid bookstall an application for permission was also made on 19th September, 2026 and an amount was also deposited with the Kolkata Municipal Corporation for grant of such permission. Therefore, by the aforesaid acts of the petitioner, itself proves that obtaining permission is mandatory before running of the bookstall, and therefore, such application was made. The receipt showing of depositing money was accepted subject to police permission. In the present case, it is admitted fact that no permission was granted to the petitioner for running the bookstall."Placing reliance on a similar order, Justice Roy dismissed the case holding that the CPI(M) was not entitled to the reliefs prayed for since no explicit permission was granted. Advocate Abhijit Mondal appeared for CPI(M). [Read Order]

title: Lawyer can't be faulted for asking NCLT to upload its order on website: NCLAT
summary: The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) recently held that an advocate cannot be faulted for sending an email to the court master of the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) requesting that a judicial order passed by NCLT be uploaded on its website [Mrinal Vs Hynite]The order copy had remained unavailable for 18 days after the pronouncement.A bench of Judicial Member Justice Mohammad Faiz Alam Khan and Technical Member Naresh Salecha deleted the adverse remarks made by the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) against advocate Mrinal Harsh Vardhan, who had emailed the NCLT court master asking that the order be uploaded.The NCLAT found that the email was polite and merely reflected the advocate's anxiety to obtain the order."Naturally when the order which was pronounced in the open Court on 05.06.2026 could not be uploaded for 18 days, we do not find any error in the act of the Appellant in sending an e-mail to the Court Master of the concerned Bench, requesting only for the uplodation of the order which was admittedly pronounced in the open Court on 05.06.2026," the NCLAT observed.The case arose from insolvency proceedings concerning Hynite Farms Private Limited.On June 5, the NCLT pronounced an order concerning the approval of a resolution plan. However, the order was not uploaded for several days.Vardhan, who represented the Resolution Professional, subsequently emailed the Court Master requesting that the same be published on the NCLT website.The email explained that the order was urgently required to implement the approved resolution plan, particularly in view of Supreme Court directions requiring coordination with the NOIDA authority.However, the NCLT made adverse observations concerning the advocate's conduct in its orders dated June 5 and July 6.Aggrieved, Vardhan approached the NCLAT, arguing that the email was neither scandalous nor improper. He also submitted that the remarks could adversely affect his professional reputation and had been made without hearing him.The respondents did not oppose his request.After examining the email, the NCLAT agreed that the advocate had done nothing wrong."We have also perused the e-mail which clearly shows that the language of the same is quite soft," the NCLAT observed.It also noted that the order had not been uploaded for 18 days despite being pronounced in open court.Accordingly, the NCLAT expunged the adverse observations while clarifying that its decision could not be relied upon in other pending contempt of court proceedings.The appellant was represented by advocates Chitranshul Sinha, Aaditya Mishra, Srishti Aggarwal and Aayushi Kiran.Advocate Sajeev Deora appeared for the Resolution Professional while advocates Rishi Singhal and Tannu Rana represented Hynite Farms.[Read Judgment]

title: Police misusing NDPS Act in cases involving codeine cough syrup: Patna High Court
summary: The Patna High Court recently criticised the police for routinely registering cases under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act when cough syrups containing codeine are seized, despite the drug falling within the permissible concentration limits prescribed by the Central government [Bharat Kumar v. State of Bihar].Justice Ashok Kumar Pandey termed the invocation of the stringent NDPS Act in such matters strange, adding that such cases need only be dealt with under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act."Cough syrup containing codeine is only a Schedule H drug for which the shopkeeper has to maintain a register and he must be a licensed one. Such types of cases should be filed under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act. It is only a violation of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, whereas the police is invariably misusing the procedure," the Court said.Justice Ashok Kumar PandeyThe Court made the observation while dealing with a bail plea by one Bharat Kumar. Kumar was arrested in May 2026 in an NDPS case following the recovery of 484 litres of codeine-based cough syrup from a pick-up van in Bihar's Khagaria district.Kumar maintained that he had merely been standing near the vehicle and had no connection with either the vehicle or the seized cough syrup.His counsel further argued that no contraband had been recovered from his possession, that he had no criminal antecedents and that a similarly placed co-accused had already been granted bail.His counsel also invoked a Central government notification dated November 14, 1985, under which certain codeine preparations are excluded from the definition of manufactured drugs under the NDPS Act.The exemption applies to preparations containing not more than 100 milligrams of codeine per dosage unit and a concentration not exceeding 2.5 per cent, provided other prescribed conditions, including their established therapeutic use, are satisfied.Meanwhile, the State opposed the bail application, relying on the Supreme Court's judgment in Hira Singh v. Union of India, which held that the entire weight of a mixture containing a narcotic drug must be considered while determining whether the seized quantity of material falls within the commercial quantity threshold. Under Section 37 of the NDPS Act, where the seized material is of commercial quantity, bail cannot be granted unless the court is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused is not guilty of the offence and that the accused is not likely to commit any offence while on bail.The Court, however, noted that where the preparation itself does not qualify as a narcotic drug, the question of determining whether the recovered substance is of a commercial quantity or not would not arise. In this regard, it also noted the bail applicant's argument that the cough syrup recovered in the present case contained less than 2.5 per cent codeine, meaning that its seizure attracted only the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, not the NDPS Act. It proceeded to grant Kumar bail. "Before parting, it is very strange that the cases where cough syrups containing codeine are recovered, the police is invariably filing cases under N.D.P.S. Act whereas in view of the notification of Central Government (supra) concentration of codeine being less than 2.5 %, the quantity does not come under the ambit of contraband," the Court added in its October 1 order. Advocate Vijay Kishore Bharti represented the bail applicant.Additional Public Prosecutor Surendra Prasad Singh appeared for the State.[Read Judgment]

title: Won't call for protest at Jantar Mantar till it is denotified as protest site: Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka assure SEM court
summary: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) activists Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka assured a Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) court in Delhi that they will not call for any protest at Jantar Mantar till it remains a denotified protest site.Assistant Commissioner of Police (ACP) Ritu Raj, acting as the SEM, recorded their statement in the order directing their release from judicial custody. The undertaking also states that they will not commit any breach of peace and that they have full faith in the judiciary and all its instruments, including the SEM Court. "That we reiterate our undertaking and commitment towards peace, law and order, public Tranquillity and further we specifically State that we will not make any calls for protest at Janta Manar till such a time that it is de-notified in accordance with Law. That we further reiterate that any protest undertaken would be done within the four corners of the Constitution," this the complete undertaking," the undertaking recorded in the order states. The police had detained Das and Ranka on October 13 after they climbed the gates of the barricaded Jantar Mantar siteOn October 14, they were sent to judicial custody for five days. On October 19, the custody was extended for two more days.In its October 19 order, the SEM court said that Das and Ranka's conduct showed that they have no respect for the law and that there are serious concerns about them breaching peace and tranquillity. The Court said that they showed "habitualness" by calling for protest at de-notified areas. Further, the SEM rejected the sureties produced for Ranka and Das after finding them unfit. After the two-day period ended today, they were produced before the Court today.Meanwhile, Das and Ranka had also challenged the SEM court's October 19 order before the Delhi High Court.However, the writ petition was withdrawn after High Court Justice Subramonium Prasad said that the SEM Court was seized of the matter today and that a more appropriate remedy for them would be a revision plea if they do not get relief from SEM court.Advocates Abhik Chimni and Pranjal Abrol appeared for Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka before SEM court and High Court.

title: Delhi High Court protects 'Benne' restaurant trademark
summary: The Delhi High Court recently restrained a Delhi-based restaurant from using the trademark 'Benne' or 'Benne Delhi' after a trademark infringement suit was filed by Shimow Hospitality, which operates a chain of South Indian restaurants under the Benne brand.Justice Vikas Mahajan found that the balance of convenience favoured the plaintiff and that it would suffer irreparable injury if interim protection was denied.Justice Vikas MahajanThe dispute concerns the use of the word 'Benne', which means butter in Kannada and is commonly associated with the popular Bengaluru-style benne dosa. According to Shimow Hospitality, it conceptualised the Benne brand in 2023-24, drawing inspiration from Bengaluru's traditional Darshini restaurant culture. The company has five outlets, including three in Mumbai and two in Delhi NCR.Senior Advocate Chander M Lall, appearing for Shimow Hospitality, argued that the Benne trademark had acquired substantial goodwill and reputation within a relatively short period.The company alleged that it discovered in August 2026 that Benne Delhi was operating a cloud kitchen or restaurant offering identical cuisine under the same name.Chander LallShimow Hospitality alleged that the defendant's adoption of an identical mark for identical services was intended to benefit from its established goodwill and could mislead consumers into believing that the two businesses were connected.After considering the submissions and documents, the Court restrained Benne Delhi and persons acting on its behalf from using the marks 'BENNE', 'BENNE DELHI' or any identical or deceptively similar mark in connection with its business.The injunction will remain operative until the next date of hearing on February 9, 2027.Lall was briefed by Advocates Shikha Sachdeva, Mugdha Palsule, Kranav Kapur and Saksham Goyal.[Read Order]

title: Only Supreme Court can say its judgment will not be cited as precedent: Delhi High Court
summary: The Delhi High Court recently held that only the Supreme Court can give a caveat that its judgment will not be cited as a precedent. A Division Bench of Justices C Hari Shankar and Vinod Kumar said that such a power is not available to any other court. “This caveat is, therefore, unique to the Supreme Court, as its decisions are constitutionally binding by virtue of Article 141 of the Constitution of India,” the Bench explained. It said that even if the facts of a case are similar to those in an earlier Supreme Court judgment, a lower court cannot treat that judgment as binding precedent if the Supreme Court itself has clarified that it should not apply in such circumstances. In such cases, the binding effect of Article 141 of the Constitution would not apply.Further, the Bench reasoned that if other courts say that their judgments will not be cited as a precedent, it could result in a situation in which similarly placed litigants would receive different treatment. “Ex facie, this would be impermissible,” the Court added. Justice C Hari Shankar and Justice Vinod KumarThe High Court rendered these observations as it upheld a Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) order. The CAT had granted a retired Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) scientist ante-dated in situ promotion under the Flexible Complementing Scheme (FCS). The Court ruled that his further promotion must still be assessed.Notably, the Central government had challenged the CAT order before the High Court, arguing that the recruitment rules and Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) memoranda bar retrospective promotion. It was also that the FCS is a merit-based scheme requiring screening, interview and committee assessment.However, the High Court rejected this argument. It held that the case was covered by a Supreme Court’s and its own ruling in Nakul Dev v Union of India. Pertinently, it was the Nakul Dev judgment of the High Court which carried a caveat that it could not be cited as precedent. The Central government had relied on this judgment. CGSC Balendu Shekhar with advocates Krishna Chaitanya and Divyansh Singh Dev appeared for Union of India. Advocates Sudarshan Rajan, Hitain Bajaj and Ria Setiya appeared for respondent Om Prakash.[Read Judgment]
